customerJourneyStories.name: From daily nurse visits to confident self-dosing at home
customerJourneyStories.summary: A patient who has relied on carers to hand out pills learns to take medication independently with the dispensing device, without feeling abandoned by the care service.

stages.narrative: The patient's medication list has grown complex and the home-care service can no longer sustain multiple daily visits just to hand out pills.

The patient and their family first hear about automated dispensing from their home-care nurse or municipality: a locked device that reminds them and dispenses the right dose, with a carer alerted if anything is missed. Discovery is the awareness moment, not the task itself: they connect the idea to staying independent at home rather than moving into care.

The patient and family weigh whether they can trust a machine with life-critical medication: is it simple enough to use, will a real person still respond, and does it reduce rather than remove human contact. They agree to try it once they see the missed-dose safety net and that the nurse stays in the loop.

A nurse installs the device, loads the first pouch roll, and walks the patient through a few dispensing cycles. The patient tests whether the prompts are clear and the confirmation button is easy to press.

Over the first weeks the patient settles into the rhythm: prompts arrive on time, the correct pouch is released on confirmation, and the household adjusts to fewer fixed-time visits while feeling safely covered.
When the routine proves reliable and the patient regains a sense of control and privacy, both patient and family come to depend on the service and resist going back to manual pill handling.

customerJourneyStories.name: A morning round that happens from the office, not the road
customerJourneyStories.summary: A nurse who once spent the morning driving between homes to hand out pills now runs the same round as a monitored caseload, driving out only to the clients who need it.

stages.narrative: The district's caseload has grown faster than staffing, and routine medication rounds are consuming the hours needed for genuine care.

The nurse is introduced to remote medication monitoring during a service rollout: dispensing runs in the home, and the portal shows who is safe and who needs attention. Discovery is the awareness moment, not the task itself: they see how it could replace routine visits with targeted response.

The nurse tests whether the alarms are trustworthy and specific enough to act on without seeing the patient, and whether the record stands up for accountability. Trust in the safety net and the audit trail decides adoption.
With a first cohort of clients on devices, the nurse runs a parallel round: monitoring in the portal while still spot-checking in person, calibrating when a remote resolution is enough.
The morning becomes a portal triage: clear clients pass untouched, alarms are worked remotely first, and only genuine needs pull the nurse onto the road, with every action logged automatically.
As reclaimed hours turn into capacity for more clients and better care, the nurse relies on the service as the backbone of safe medication across the district.

Armed with population-level safety and savings evidence, the manager secures renewal and expansion, and the service becomes core infrastructure for the care organisation.
